## 1. Open and Visualise Raster Data

<details>
<summary> Adding a raster layer in QGIS:</summary>

- Open QGIS.
- Click Layer (top menu).
- Select Add Layer → Add Raster Layer
- Click Browse.
- Navigate to your raster file (e.g., .tif, .img, .asc).
- Select the file.
- Click Open.
- Click Add.

</details>

<details>
<summary> Plot Raster: </summary>

- Select Raster Properties 
- Symbology
- Render Type: Single Band Pseudo Color
- Select required color ramp for plotting DEM
- What color ramp is best for Plotting the DEM?

<img src="Week3_SS/1.jpg" width="400">

</details>

<details>
<summary> Just for fun: Visualize your DEM in 3D: </summary>

- Go to View option
- Select 3D Map View > New 3D Map
- Click on the setting icon
- Select DEM as the Terrain
- Optionally, Hillshade can be added for better shading
- Hold the shift key and toggle with mouse for a fully interactive 3D Map
- How are the results affected when changing the vertical scale of the 3D Map?

<img src="Week3_SS/2.jpg" width="400">

</details>

## 2. Create a point vector dataset by importing a table
<details>
<summary> Open the file stations_bawue_montly_temp.csv: </summary>

- Layer > Add Layer > Add Delimited Text Layer
- Select stations_bawue_montly_temp.csv
- In File Format > Select Custom Delimiters > Tick Semicolon
- In Geometry Definitions > Select Point Co-ordinates
- X Field = Lon - Y Field = Lat
- Click Add

</details>

<details>
<summary> View the Data Table </summary>
- Right click on csv file
- Open attribute table

</details>

<details>
<summary> Access Longitude and Latitude of a specific station: </summary>
- Open Attribute Table of the csv file added
- Select by Expression (ε icon) 
- Type "Station" = 257
- Click Select
- The station will be shown on the map

<img src="Week3_SS/3.jpg" width="400">

</details>

<details>
<summary> Plot Station Locations and convert in vector points: </summary>
- Select Processing > Toolbox > Create Points Layers from Table
- Input your csv file
- Select X field = Lon - Y field = Lat
- All station locations are plotted in vector format
- Export the newly formed vector data in 'ESRI Shapefile' format
- Is the newly formed vector point file visible on QGIS? If not, explain why?   
**Hint:** Check Longitude and Latitude
<!--
- Fix lattitude and longitude by going in the field calculator for the excel data added and using the expression: to_real(replace("latitude", ',', '.'))
- This converts the , into . for creating vector points from csv
-->

</details>

<details>
<summary> Plot the final raster with vector points: </summary>
- Vector point layer must be above the raster layer
- Change can be made to both the raster data and vector point data in properties by editing colour, contrast and hue through symbology

<img src="Week3_SS/3.1.jpg" width="400">

</details>

<details>

## 4. Projections, transformations and subsetting

<details>
<summary> Convert Raster to binary mask layer: </summary>
- Raster > Raster Calculator
- Enter Expression ("YOUR_DEM" >= 0)
- What does this do? Explain your results.

</details>

<details>
<summary> Polygonize the Raster: </summary>
- Raster > Conversion > Polygonize (Raster to Vector)
- Select the newly created boundary DEM file 
- Click Run

</details>

<details>
<summary> Clip polygons into the DEM boundary: </summary>
- Vector > Geoprocessing Tools > Clip
- Input Layer = District Boundary 
- Overlay Layer = Raster boundary polygon (VECTORIZED)
- Click Run

<img src="Week3_SS/6.jpg" width="400">

</details>

## 5. Intersection of Raster Layers and Vector Data

<details>
<summary> Calculate the mean height of each municipality where a meteorological station is present within the DEM: </summary>
- Open Geoprocessing Toolbox > Raster Analysis > Zonal Statistics
- Input Layer = Clipped Municipality Polygons
- Raster Layer = DEM 
- Statistics to Calculate = Mean (You can also add min, max, median etc for further analysis)
- Add a Output column prefix (Eg: DEM_)
- Run
- A new Vector file is produced with an added column, which shows the mean height for each meteorological station

<img src="Week3_SS/7.jpg" width="400">

</details>

<details>
<summary> Plot a diagram: </summary>
- Open properties for the new vector file with mean height data > Diagrams 
- Select Histogram of bar chart 
- Value = DEM_mean
- Mean height diagram plotted on the polygon.
- **Hint:** Alternatively you can also use the **Data Plotly** plugin in QGIS for better Plots.

<img src="Week3_SS/8.jpg" width="400">

</details>

<details>
<summary> Plot a map with all polygons lower than 700 m a.s.l displayed as black polygons, all the other polygons in red colour: </summary>
- Open symbology for vector layer containing calculated mean height
- At the top dropdown select **Rule-Based**
- Add a new rule
- Label = < 700m
- Filter expression: "DEM_mean" < 700
- Set fill colour to black
- Repeat the process for heights above 700m.
- What would the Filter Expression be for heights above 700m?

<img src="Week3_SS/9.jpg" width="400">

</details>


## Homework

<details>
<summary> 1. Intersection of raster and vector data [Points] </summary>

We only have the temperature values for some weather stations that are scattered across the DEM. To create a spatially explicit raster of temperature, we will use the well-known relationship of air temperature and elevation which often show a high inverse correlation.

Hence, implement a linear regression between DEM heights and temperature values from January 2016 and use this model to perform a simplistic temperature interpolation. Follow the steps below.

- Extract DEM values at the point data coordinates as vector layer dem.heights using extract().

<!-- Go to Toolbox > Raster Analysis > Sample Raster Values
Input Raster = DEM
Input Layer = Points from Table

The resulting output creates a new vector point where a new column is generated for the DEM value at each specific station.
--> 

- Save the temperature data from January 2016 named temp_2016_1 to a numeric vector.

<!-- Use Refactor Tool to fix 2016_1 to convert it into point instead of a comma. 
Using the expression: to_real(replace("2016_1", ',', '.'))
-->

- Plot both numeric vectors in a scatterplot.

<!-- Use Plotly  in QGIS to create scatterplot, using DEM_val as x or y axis and 2016_1 as x or y axis
-->

- Calculate the correlation and the coefficient of determination (r^2). Use the argument corr("DEM_val", "temp_2016_1") in field calculator for your point layer. Why is this argument necessary?

- Detect the linear regression coefficients using the function lm(y ~ x). Which vector is y, which vector is x? Where is gain and offset stored within the resulting object?

- Add the regression line to the scatterplot using abline().

- Summary of the model

- The coefficients are saved in lin_model$coefficients. How to get the intercept and gain of the linear model?

- Interpolate the temperature data of our study area based on the linear model coefficients you just derived. Hint: It is not necessary to use functions such as predict(). You may apply simple algebra with raster data: e.g.if you would like to transform the height of the DEM from m to cm, simply calculate height.in.cm <- DEM/100

- **Hint:** predict() will not work here as a function based on lm(). We will use the function predict() at a later stage…

- Plot your results in a map.

</details>

<details>
<summary> 2. Intersection of Raster and Vector Data: </summary>

- Open the polygon dataset AX_KommunalesGebiet.shp in QGIS.

- Determine how many polygons the dataset contains.

- Create a new empty field in the attribute table to store mean elevation values for each polygon.

<details>
<summary> For each polygon in the dataset: </summary>

- Extract the raster values from the DEM that fall within the polygon boundaries
- Calculate the mean elevation of those raster values
- Store the calculated mean value in the corresponding attribute field of that polygon

</details>

- Ensure that all polygons in the dataset are processed so that each polygon has an associated mean elevation value.
- After completing the calculations, join or keep the computed mean elevation values in the polygon attribute table.
- Visualize the resulting mean elevation values on a map using an appropriate classification method (for example, graduated colors).

</details>
